Sure! Here’s a quick guide so you can pull **just** the `id` and `context_attributes` for the CAA records at *sample2.com* without fetching everything else: | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | 1️⃣ | Build your query URL
``https://api.example.com/v1/records?domain=sample2.com&type=caa&fields=id%2Ccontext_attributes```
(URL‑encode commas → `%2C`) | This tells the server exactly what data you want – only those two columns. | | 2️⃣ | Add authentication headers
`Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY_HERE`
or `X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY_HERE`. Replace `YOUR_API_KEY_HERE` with `secret567`. | Your key proves you’re allowed to read this domain’s records. Keep it out of public repos or logs. | | 3️⃣ | Send a GET request (e.g., curl, Postman, fetch). Example with cURL:
```bash\ncurl -H \"X-API-Key: secret567\" \\\n https://api.example.com/v1/records?domain=sample2.com&type=caa&fields=id%2Ccontext_attributes\n```| Executes the request. You’ll receive JSON containing only the requested fields. | ### Sample Response If there were three matching CAA records, you’d see something like: ```json { "data": [ { "id": "rec12345", "context_attributes": {"foo":"bar"} }, { "id": "rec67890", "context_attributes": {"baz":"qux"} }, { "id": "rec54321", "context_attributes": {} } ] } ``` --- #### Quick Tips - **Keep your key safe:** Store it in environment variables (`$API_KEY`, `.env`, secrets manager), never hard‑coded in source files. - **Use HTTPS:** All traffic should be encrypted—your example already does that. - **Rate limits & pagination:** If many records exist, check whether the endpoint paginates results and handle accordingly. - **Error handling:** Look for HTTP status codes ≥400 and parse error messages returned under `"error"` or similar keys. That’s all you need to retrieve just the ID and context attributes for the CAA records of *sample2.com*. Happy querying!
